946.title: The Light of Asia
946.hook: Edwin Arnold's long poem of the Buddha's life, told in English verse
946.carry: a dewdrop slipping into the shining sea
946.howItsDone: The Light of Asia is no longer a scripture anyone practices from, but it is still read as literature, and some Western Buddhists and readers of Buddhism remember it as the book that first introduced them to the Buddha's life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Max Müller and the translators who carried the texts into French and English. Your line: into English.

What happens when the Buddha's story leaves the scholar's desk and lands in a parlor? A translation of the Dhammapada is careful, scholarly work. But an English poet and newspaperman named Edwin Arnold had a different idea. He would tell the whole life of the Buddha as a long poem: the palace, the four sights, the night he left, the tree, the awakening, the teaching. In English verse, for ordinary readers.
screen: `FROM THE DESK TO THE PARLOR.` → `A WHOLE LIFE AS A POEM.` → `FOR ORDINARY READERS.`

segments.voice: The Light of Asia is not a translation of any one scripture. It's an original English poem, in long, rolling lines, drawing on the traditional stories of the Buddha's life. Its subtitle calls it The Great Renunciation, and Arnold presents it as told by an Indian Buddhist, so the voice is meant to be a believer's, speaking with love. The story is one this path has told already. The young prince Siddhartha grows up in a palace where sorrow is hidden from him. He sees age, sickness, death, and a wandering holy man. He leaves his sleeping wife and child in the night, searches, nearly starves, sits beneath the tree, and wakes up. Then he teaches. The poem tells it with color: gardens, music, horses, moonlight. Near the end, after the teaching of nirvana, Arnold leaves a picture: a dewdrop slipping into the shining sea. A small, bright thing letting go of its edges and becoming part of something vast. Readers have argued about whether that's what nirvana means, and Buddhist teachers explain it in different ways. But the picture stayed with people. For some readers in Britain and America, this poem was their first meeting with the Buddha at all, not as a curiosity but as a teacher worth loving. It's long and old-fashioned, and critics have called it more Victorian than Indian in places. Still, it carried the story into homes the scholars never reached.

947.title: Chicago, 1893
947.hook: at the World's Parliament of Religions, Dharmapala and the Zen teacher Soyen Shaku speak
947.howItsDone: Buddhists in Sri Lanka honor Anagarika Dharmapala as a reviver of the teaching and of the sites in India, and Japanese Zen remembers Soyen Shaku as a teacher who brought Zen before Western listeners.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a long poem carried the Buddha's life to English readers. Your line: a dewdrop slipping into the shining sea.
screen: `A DEWDROP SLIPPING INTO THE SHINING SEA.`

segments.voice: A big hall in Chicago, a long row of speakers on the stage. People of many faiths have been invited to stand up, one after another, and explain their own tradition to a crowd of strangers. Some in the seats have read about the Buddha in books like yesterday's poem. Now a Buddhist stands in front of them: a young man from Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, in a plain white robe, Anagarika Dharmapala. Beside him on the program, a Zen abbot from Japan named Soyen Shaku.
screen: `A HALL IN CHICAGO.` → `FAITHS ON ONE STAGE.` → `TWO BUDDHIST VOICES.`

segments.voice: It was called the World's Parliament of Religions, and it met alongside a great fair in Chicago. Its organizers wanted the religions of the world side by side, each in its own words, and they printed the speeches afterward, so we can still read them. Dharmapala had spent his young life working to restore Buddhist places in India, above all Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha woke up under the tree. In Chicago he spoke of the Buddha as a teacher of reason and kindness, whose way was open to anyone willing to practice it. Soyen Shaku was the abbot of a Zen temple in Kamakura, and he did not speak English. His talk, on cause and effect, was put into English and read to the hall for him. Accounts say a young lay student of his helped with the English: D. T. Suzuki, who comes back tomorrow. Why it matters: some in that hall had met the Buddha only in books by outsiders. Here, Buddhists spoke for themselves. The Dhammapada has a line that fits a week of long speeches: "Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet." In a hall full of speeches, that was the hope.

948.title: Zen comes west
948.hook: teachers like D. T. Suzuki carry Zen to Western readers
948.howItsDone: Zen communities in the West sit together in meditation halls, often under teachers trained in Japan or in lineages that came from there, and read short Zen stories as part of their study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chicago, and two Buddhist voices on one stage. Your line: the teaching speaks.

A story told in Zen circles. A learned visitor comes to a Zen teacher to ask about Zen. The teacher serves tea, pouring into the cup until it's full, and keeps pouring. Tea runs over the rim and across the table. Stop, says the visitor, nothing more will go in. Like this cup, the teacher answers, you are full of your own opinions. How can I show you Zen unless you first empty your cup? Stories like that crossed the ocean in books, and some Western readers met Zen first on the page.
screen: `A CUP OF TEA.` → `IT OVERFLOWS.` → `FIRST, EMPTY YOUR CUP.`

segments.voice: Remember the young layman who helped Soyen Shaku with his English in Chicago? D. T. Suzuki had trained in Zen under that abbot in Kamakura. Afterward he went to America and spent years there translating and writing. He wrote about Zen in English, in essays and translations, and later lectured to university audiences. Readers who had never met a Zen teacher met Zen through him: the sudden awakenings, the strange questions, the teachers who answered with a shout. What crossed most easily were the short stories, like the cup of tea. Zen describes itself with a saying tradition gives to Bodhidharma, whom we met on the road through China: a special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words, pointing straight at the mind. There's a gentle joke in that. A tradition that says it doesn't depend on words reached the West through a great many of them. But Zen keeps pointing past the book. The stories are meant to unsettle the mind that thinks it already knows, and the tradition's answer to that unsettled mind is to sit. So the books were followed by people. Japanese teachers came west to lead sittings, and Western students went to Japan to train in monasteries and came home to teach. A cup of tea in a book, then real cups of tea in real meditation halls, across the ocean.

949.title: Temples in the West
949.hook: Japanese American temples, including through the wartime internment camps where practice continued
949.howItsDone: Japanese American Buddhist temples, including Jodo Shinshu temples, hold regular services, Sunday schools and a summer Obon festival with dancing, and some communities hold pilgrimages to the sites of the wartime camps.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Suzuki carried Zen west in books, and in a cup of tea that overflowed. Your line: across the ocean.

A Sunday morning in a plain wooden barracks. Benches in rows. A small altar built by hand, an incense bowl, a priest in robes, and families chanting together. Outside the door: a fence, and a guard tower. During the Second World War, the United States government forced Japanese Americans from their homes on the West Coast and held them in camps. Among the things people carried in with them was their Buddhist practice. Inside the fence, it kept going.
screen: `A SERVICE IN A BARRACKS.` → `A FENCE OUTSIDE.` → `PRACTICE KEPT GOING.`

segments.voice: Japanese families who settled in Hawaii and on the American mainland built temples, among them temples of Jodo Shinshu, the Pure Land school of Shinran we met in Japan. These were family temples: services, funerals, Sunday schools for the children, and the summer Obon festival, when the dead are remembered and the community dances together in the street. When war came between the United States and Japan, Buddhist priests, as community leaders, were among those taken away for questioning and detention. Then whole families, citizens and not, were removed to camps in the interior. Temples were closed, and some families hid or left behind their home altars. In the camps, people organized Buddhist services, held funerals, ran Sunday schools and youth groups, and danced Obon in the dust between the barracks. They said the nembutsu, Namu Amida Butsu, entrusting themselves to Amida Buddha. At a camp in Utah, during those years, the mainland temple association took the name Buddhist Churches of America, and it still goes by that name. After the camps closed, families came home, reopened temples, and started again. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words, has a picture of steadiness that fits: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." Wind on every side, and with their temples shut, the communities kept their ground.

950.title: Tibetan teachers in exile
950.hook: after 1959 Tibetan teachers settle in India, then teach worldwide
950.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists in exile keep up their monasteries, schools and debate in India and Nepal, and Tibetan teachers lead centers around the world where students study and practice in their lineages.

segments.voice: Yesterday: temples in the West, and services held inside a fence. Your line: kept their ground.

A high mountain pass, snow to the knees, thin air. A monk walks it with a bundle tied to his back: a few long, loose-leaf texts wrapped in cloth, the kind we saw in the Tibetan canons. Behind him are the monasteries where he learned to read them. Ahead, the foothills of India, a country he has never seen. When the Dalai Lama left Tibet for India, monks, nuns, teachers and families followed him over passes like this one, on foot.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN PASS.` → `TEXTS TIED TO HIS BACK.` → `INTO INDIA.`

segments.voice: The Dalai Lama settled in Dharamsala, a hill town in the north of India, and it became the center of Tibetan life in exile, with its own offices, schools, temples and a library for Tibetan texts. Monks who made it across rebuilt their great monasteries in settlements in southern India, on farmland far from the snow. Sera, Drepung and Ganden, names from the hills around Lhasa, rose again there, and the debate courtyards came back too: monks clapping and questioning each other in the afternoon, as they had at home. In exile, teachers met students from everywhere. Lamas from the Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug schools traveled to Europe, North America, Asia and beyond, and founded centers where people who had never seen Tibet learned its chants, meditations and texts. A refugee may have to leave almost everything behind. These teachers carried the teaching in memory, in practice, and in those loose-leaf texts on their backs. In the last year of the Buddha's life, as Rhys Davids' translation of the Book of the Great Decease tells it, he gave this advice to Ananda: "be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves." A refuge you can carry. For teachers who lost their monasteries, their country and their road home, that is what the teaching had to become, and what they handed on to students they could never have pictured meeting.

951.title: Insight goes west
951.hook: Burmese and Thai meditation methods reach Western lay students
951.howItsDone: Insight meditation students sit and walk in silence, noting what arises, often on retreats at centers in the Burmese or Thai lineages, and Theravada monasteries in the West also teach meditation to laypeople.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dharamsala, and Tibetan teachers who carried a whole tradition over the mountains. Your line: teaching in exile.

Rising. Falling. Rising. Falling. In a meditation hall in Yangon, a student sits with her attention on her belly, silently naming each movement as the breath comes and goes. A sound outside: hearing. A thought about lunch: thinking. Back to rising, falling. Her teacher's instruction is short: know what is happening, while it's happening. No robes required, no years in a monastery first. That simple method, and other ways of sitting from Burma and Thailand, traveled to lay students on the other side of the world.
screen: `RISING, FALLING.` → `HEARING. THINKING.` → `KNOW IT AS IT HAPPENS.`

segments.voice: In Burma, teachers began to teach meditation to ordinary laypeople, not only to monks and nuns. Ledi Sayadaw wrote and taught for lay students, and later Mahasi Sayadaw opened a center in Yangon where anyone could come and practice. The Mahasi way is noting: a soft mental label for whatever is happening, moment by moment. It rests on an old teaching, the sutta on the setting up of mindfulness. There, the Buddha says a practitioner who is walking knows, I am walking, and who is standing knows, I am standing, and so with sitting and lying down. Know the body as body, feelings as feelings, the mind as mind. The Pali for the clear seeing that grows from this is vipassana, insight. In Thailand, forest monks like Ajahn Chah taught in simple monasteries among the trees. Western men came to him, ordained, and some went on to found monasteries in England and elsewhere. And Western students who had sat in Burma, Thailand and India came home and taught insight meditation in plain retreat centers, often to people who called themselves nothing in particular. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words, opens its chapter on earnestness like this: "Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvâna), thoughtlessness the path of death." Rising, falling, hearing, thinking. Small, earnest noting, carried across the world.

chat.says: In noting meditation, what do I do when a thought about lunch pops up?
options: Note it softly, thinking, then come back to rising and falling.
Push it away firmly, since thoughts mean the sitting has failed.
Follow it to the end, so the mind runs out of thoughts by itself.
chat.meaning: Noting gives whatever happens a soft label, hearing, thinking, and then returns to the belly. You just know what is happening, while it's happening.

952.title: Everywhere now
952.hook: Buddhist communities in Europe, Africa, Latin America and beyond
952.carry: a good man pervades every place
952.howItsDone: Buddhist communities around the world gather in temples, monasteries and meditation centers, from family temples of immigrant communities to centers founded by Western students and temples built abroad by Asian orders.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vipassana went west, rising, falling, hearing, thinking. Your line: insight travels.

Three postcards. From Brazil: a temple in São Paulo, incense, a family bowing before a Japanese altar, and a conversation in Portuguese afterward over tea. From South Africa: a large temple with curved roofs on the grass near Pretoria, built by a Buddhist order from Taiwan. From Germany: a quiet house on a hill on the northern edge of Berlin, with steps up to a shrine room, where monks from Sri Lanka live. Three continents, one teaching.
screen: `A TEMPLE IN SÃO PAULO.` → `A TEMPLE NEAR PRETORIA.` → `A HOUSE IN BERLIN.`

segments.voice: When people move, their practice moves with them. Japanese families in Brazil built temples, just as they did in Hawaii and California. Sri Lankan, Thai, Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean and Tibetan communities have done the same in cities across Europe, the Americas, Africa and Australia, sometimes starting in a living room before there was a building. Others came to the teaching through books and travel. In Berlin, a doctor named Paul Dahlke built a house for Buddhist practice, and it still stands as a temple. And some Asian orders built temples abroad on purpose. The Taiwanese order Fo Guang Shan built Nan Hua Temple in South Africa, near Pretoria, and from it monks and nuns have taught in other parts of Africa. Look at the road since the poem. The Light of Asia put the Buddha's life into English verse. In Chicago, the teaching spoke for itself. Zen came west in a cup of tea. Temples kept their practice going behind a fence. Tibetan teachers carried a tradition over the mountains. Insight came west as noting. And now, everywhere. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words, compares the good to a scent that goes where flowers can't, and ends the verse: "a good man pervades every place." A teaching that began on foot in northern India now has shrine rooms on continents far from where it began.
screen: `FAMILIES BRING THEIR TEMPLES.` · `SEEKERS BUILD CENTERS.` · `ORDERS SEND TEACHERS.` · `A WEEK OF CROSSINGS.` · then, large: `EVERYWHERE NOW.`

segments.voice: Choose a place far from where you're sitting, and picture a small shrine room there, a few people sitting, maybe at this very hour, in a language you don't speak. Breathe in, and know they're breathing too. Breathe out, and sit with them across the distance.
Everywhere now. Temples in São Paulo, near Pretoria and in Berlin, built by families, seekers and orders, far from where the teaching began.
Your line: a good man pervades every place. Like a scent, it goes where flowers can't. Another week, done.

what it means: families, seekers and orders have planted temples in Europe, Africa, Latin America and beyond.
what a scholar hears: three routes at once: immigrant family temples, centers founded by converts, and temples built abroad by Asian orders like Fo Guang Shan.
recall: an Afghan valley where two Buddhas stood

chat.says: How did Buddhist temples end up in places like Brazil and South Africa?
options: Families brought practice when they moved; seekers and Asian orders built too.
Western governments built them to welcome visitors from Asian countries.
They're mostly museums, built to show Buddhist art to people far away.
chat.meaning: Three routes: families brought their temples when they moved, seekers like Paul Dahlke built centers, and orders like Fo Guang Shan sent teachers abroad.
